notes: Derivation from the read lineage-reads-1985/s-101.json: CONFORMS on a unpopulatable-antecedent derivation of its own (docs/CONFORMANCE.md section 8, DRV-1985-SR-IV.4.1-p3); the code location is where the compiler meets the rule's subject. The read: The antecedent is 'When a character set contains fewer than 52 characters (all characters of the COBOL character set except the lowercase letters)'; only then 'double characters must be substituted for the single characters' (the obsolete feature, C.1(1)). The character set a program is written in is whatever SourceTextDecoder.Decode reads the file as, and that is a closed set: UCS in UTF-8/16/32 or ISO/IEC 8859-1, never a smaller set (a malformed marked file yields no text at all, error COBOL5434). ISO/IEC 8859-1 has 256 characters and UCS more; each contains the 26 uppercase letters, 10 digits and 16 special characters at their ASCII code points, so the count is never below 52 and no double-character substitution is ever required or recognized. The run-time side does not reopen it: alphanumeric data is held as UTF-16 / ISO/IEC 8859-1 bytes (DRV-GR-8.1.3.2-5, docs/conformance/8), also at least 256 characters. Being obsolete changes nothing here: the high-subset compiler need not provide a feature whose condition cannot occur. Witnessed on the train85b-rows build: E:/COBOL-coord/scratch/w20262131/last2/probes/cset85.cob uses all 78 characters of the 1985 COBOL character set in program text outside literals (lowercase and uppercase words, digits, space, + - * / = in COMPUTE, $ and , . in a PICTURE, ; and , as separators, " as literal delimiter, ( ) : in a reference modifier, > < in a condition) and runs identically in all three reading families: unmarked UTF-8 (runs/cset85-001), UTF-16LE with mark (probes/cset85u16.cob, runs/cset85u16-001) and ISO/IEC 8859-1 (probes/cset85l1.cob, an 0xA4 byte in a comment line forces the Latin-1 reading and draws COBOL5435; runs/cset85l1-001): each prints ARITH OK +0619, EDIT $1,234.50, REFMOD 2345 and the 52 letters, exit 0.
